segments.literal: and-made-grow the-LORD God from-the-ground every-of tree desirable for-sight and-good for-food and-tree-of the-life in-midst-of the-garden and-tree-of the-knowledge good and-evil

construct; כָּל־ binds to the next word
collective-singular use: 'every tree'
Niphal participle of חמד: 'to be desired'
לְ + מַרְאֶה: literally 'for sight'

construct state

construct; Rashi: בָּאֶמְצַע
construct, with the second noun lacking its own head: see Ibn Ezra
דַּעַת

phrases.literal: 'and-made-grow the-LORD God'; wayyiqtol Hiphil, causative of 'sprout'

phrases.english: desirable to look at and good for food
phrases.literal: 'desirable for-sight and-good for-food'; two predicates sharing 'tree'

phrases.english: and the tree of life in the middle of the garden
and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil
phrases.literal: 'and-tree-of the-knowledge good and-evil'; 'knowledge' read as the head of the construct, with 'good and evil' as its content, following Ibn Ezra

grammar: וַיַּצְמַח is a wayyiqtol Hiphil: the LORD God is the cause of the growth.
נֶחְמָד is a Niphal participle: 'desirable' (literally 'being desired'); it and טוֹב are both adjectival predicates of עֵץ.
The etnaḥta on לְמַאֲכָל ends the first half: all trees; the second half names the two special trees.
עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע: the Hebrew has no word between הַדַּעַת and טוֹב. The construct chain is elliptical, 'tree of the knowledge (of) good and evil'.
Ibn Ezra's reading: the text means 'the tree of the knowledge, the knowledge of good and evil' (he compares הָאָרוֹן הַבְּרִית), which is how the English line is built.
segments.note: בְּתוֹךְ is rendered 'in the middle of' with Rashi and Radak (Targum Onkelos: בִּמְצִיעוּת גִּנְּתָא). Whether both trees stand at the one point or the middle is a broad area (Ramban) is left open by the Hebrew. 'Knowledge' stays a bare noun, 'of good and evil' being its content, following Ibn Ezra's supplied 'knowledge'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the verse speaks of the garden; the growth is that of the trees in Eden, not of the earth at large.
Rashi glosses בְּתוֹךְ as בָּאֶמְצַע, 'in the middle'.
Ibn Ezra: when He caused every tree to sprout from the ground, so it grew in the garden, and in addition two trees in its midst.

Ibn Ezra: one must supply 'knowledge': 'and the tree of the knowledge, the knowledge of good and evil', since the noun cannot be bound to a word already known; he compares הָאָרוֹן הַבְּרִית and הַנְּבוּאָה עֹדֵד הַנָּבִיא.
Ramban: the trees stand in a broad central plot (translating Onkelos בִּמְצִיעוּת גִּנְּתָא); he rejects the view that the fruit of knowledge aroused sexual desire.
Radak: the trees were lovely in height, leaves and species, and their fruit good to eat; the garden is reserved for the messianic age.

apparatus: No textual variant in this verse; the pack reports none.

segments.english: A river flows out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divides and becomes four headwaters.
segments.literal: and-river going-out from-Eden to-water ACC the-garden and-from-there it-divides and-became into-four heads

tokens.note: ו introduces a new scene; no verb 'was' is needed
participle: continuing action, 'a river is going out'
Hiphil infinitive construct of שקה, 'to give drink to', with ל of purpose
marks the garden as direct object
Niphal imperfect of פרד: 'it separates itself'
perfect with ו: the sequence continues after the yiqtol
לְ + number: 'become four'
literally 'heads': heads of the four streams that begin there

phrases.english: A river flows out of Eden

phrases.literal: 'and-became into-four heads'; 'heads' as the starting points of the four rivers, per Radak

grammar: יֹצֵא is a participle with no auxiliary: the river is going out of Eden as a standing fact.
לְהַשְׁקוֹת is Hiphil: 'to cause to drink', hence 'to water'.
יִפָּרֵד is Niphal (it is separated, it splits), and וְהָיָה, a perfect with simple ו, continues the thought.
רָאשִׁים is the plural of רֹאשׁ 'head'. The four 'heads' are named in the next verses.
The pashta on וּמִשָּׁם and zaqef on יִפָּרֵד set 'from there it divides' as a unit.
segments.note: רָאשִׁים is rendered 'headwaters': the 'heads' are the four beginnings of rivers (Radak: 'parts, since each part is the head of what comes out of it'). Whether the river first enters the garden and divides after leaving it (Radak) is not stated by the Hebrew. WLC vowels the first word with a dagesh in the resh; the base text here does not (see apparatus).

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: even before the human was created the river was watering the garden on every side.
Ibn Ezra: the alef of רָאשִׁים is a root letter, as in מַרְאֲשׁוֹתֵיכֶם; the word is 'head'.
Radak: after it has watered the garden it leaves and is divided into four parts, each called a river.
Radak: רָאשִׁים means parts, because each part is the head of the stream that goes out from it.
Sforno: the river irrigated without rain or human labour; a comment on the garden's ease, not on the wording.

apparatus: 2:10.1 vowels: WLC reads וְנָהָרּ֙ (with dagesh); the base text וְנָהָר֙ is followed.
WLC note p: punctuation in L is read differently from BHS.

segments.english: The name of the first is Pishon; it is the one that encircles the whole land of Havilah, where the gold is.
segments.literal: name-of the-one Pishon he the-encircling ACC all-of land-of the-Havilah which-there the-gold

tokens.note: construct
הָאֶחָד, 'the one', used for 'the first'
a river name
הוּא as copula: 'it is'
article plus participle: 'the one that goes around'
the yetiv accent on אֵת is a stress-marking accent
construct
a land; the article is idiomatic with the name
אֲשֶׁר + שָׁם = 'where'
with the article, 'the gold' known of that land

phrases.english: The name of the first is Pishon
it is the one that encircles

phrases.literal: 'which-there the-gold'; the Hebrew has no verb

grammar: שֵׁם הָאֶחָד has no 'is': the verse is a nominal clause, 'the name of the first (river): Pishon'.
הוּא הַסֹּבֵב is a pronoun with an article-plus-participle: 'he, the encircler'.
אֲשֶׁר־שָׁם 'which-there' is the idiom for 'where'.
The revia on הַסֹּבֵב marks a pause before the object, and the zaqef on הַחֲוִילָה before the relative clause.
Each of the four names is introduced by שֵׁם and a number; the pattern runs from 2:11 to 2:14.
segments.note: The English does not identify the river. Rashi says Pishon is the Nile of Egypt, named from its rising waters or from flax (פִּשְׁתָּן); Ibn Ezra reports the Gaon's identification as the Nile, doubts it from the geography, and says it is unproved. The Hebrew gives only name, circuit and the gold of Havilah. 'Encircle' for סבב fits Qal 2.d 'surround, encompass'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: Pishon is the Nile, named for its waters rising and irrigating the land (cf. וּפָשׁוּ פָרָשָׁיו) or for flax (cf. עֹבְדֵי פִשְׁתִּים of Egypt); the identification and etymology are kept here, not in the English line.
Ibn Ezra: the Gaon says Pishon is the Nile, but the geography does not fit; the identification is unproved, so the English names none.
Ramban: this Havilah is not the Egyptian one (25:18), which lies to the east; bdellium and onyx are found in river sand, like gold.
Radak: Havilah lies near Eden and is praised for what it yields, as the garden is praised for trees and fruit.
Radak: the article on הַזָּהָב is because gold is found elsewhere too, but here it is plentiful and good.
Sforno: the verse praises the river that waters the garden by naming its branches known to us; a comment on purpose.

segments.english: The gold of that land is good; bdellium is there, and onyx stone.
segments.literal: and-gold-of the-land the-that good there the-bdellium and-stone-of the-onyx

tokens.note: construct; the lexicon lists only 'golden oil' for this entry, which does not fit; plain 'gold'
הַהִוא, feminine, agreeing with הָאָרֶץ
a resin or a small round stone: Ibn Ezra reports the Gaon's 'small round stones'
construct
שֹׁהַם: a precious stone, white and clear according to Ibn Ezra and Radak; identity uncertain

phrases.english: The gold of that land is good

phrases.literal: 'there the-bdellium'; the Hebrew has the adverb before the noun

grammar: הַהִוא is the feminine 'that', the feminine form, agreeing with הָאָרֶץ.
Both clauses are nominal: no 'is'. The etnaḥta falls after טוֹב.
שָׁם before the noun puts weight on the place: 'there is the bdellium'.
וְאֶבֶן הַשֹּׁהַם is a construct chain, 'the stone of the onyx', while בְּדֹלַח has no 'stone' (Radak: it is too small to work).
The articles on הַבְּדֹלַח and הַשֹּׁהַם present them as the known goods of that land.
segments.note: בְּדֹלַח and שֹׁהַם are of uncertain identity. Ibn Ezra and Radak take bdellium as a small round white stone (Num 11:7) and onyx as a fine white stone; the conventional 'bdellium' and 'onyx' are kept, and the other identifications are recorded here. The BDB entry for זָהָב offers only sense 10, which does not fit; the plain sense 'gold' is used. WLC vowels the first word with a hataf patah; the base text has a shewa.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: the Gaon says bdellium is small round stones coming out of the water, like the manna (Num 11:7); onyx is a precious white clear stone; we do not know their identity.
Radak: bdellium is a small white round stone, said to form from dew drops; it is strung on a thread, so the text does not say 'stone of bdellium'.
Radak: onyx is a large white pure stone used for kings' vessels; the names of Israel's sons were engraved on it.

apparatus: 2:12.1 vowels: WLC reads וּֽזֲהַ֛ב (hataf patah); the base text וּֽזְהַ֛ב is followed.

segments.english: The name of the second river is Gihon; it is the one that encircles the whole land of Cush.
segments.literal: and-name-of the-river the-second Gihon he the-encircling ACC all-of land-of Cush

tokens.note: construct, no sense listed for this use of שֵׁם beyond 'name'
Rashi: from גִּיחַ 'to burst forth, roar'
a land and people, usually south of Egypt; Rashi: written by the name it later bore

phrases.english: The name of the second river is Gihon
it is the one that encircles the whole land of Cush

grammar: The verse is a copy of 2:11 in form: name, number, 'he the encircling'.
הוּא הַסּוֹבֵב is pronoun plus article and participle, 'he who encircles'.
The silluq on כּוּשׁ closes the verse; the zaqef qaton after הַסּוֹבֵב marks the pause before the object.
Radak notes that the river does not go from one side to the others: the land itself is what is encircled.
The name גִּיחוֹן is built on גִּיחַ 'burst forth', hence Rashi's 'the one that surges and roars'.
segments.note: The name receives its meaning in Rashi (surging, roaring, from גִּיחַ) and in Radak (a river that sends out many branches); neither belongs in the English line. 'Cush' is kept as a plain transliteration. The text does not say where Cush lies; Radak puts it in the south.

commentary.summary: Rashi: Gihon is so named because it goes on, surging and roaring greatly, from גִּיחַ as in כִּי יִגַּח (Ex 21:28); the etymology is kept in the notes.
Radak: Gihon is from the sense of going forth, since it divides into many branches in the land of Cush.
Radak: the river does not go from one quarter to another; it is the land itself that is encircled.

segments.english: The name of the third river is the Tigris; it is the one that flows east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.
segments.literal: and-name-of the-river the-third Hiddekel he the-going east-of Asshur and-the-river the-fourth he Perat

tokens.note: construct
the Hebrew חִדֶּקֶל, Hiddekel; Rashi: from חַדִּין וְקַלִּין, 'sharp and swift'
participle with article: 'the one that goes'
קִדְמַת: the ת of the construct stands for the directive ה (Ibn Ezra)
אַשּׁוּר, Asshur; Rashi: not yet existing, written by its future name
pronoun as copula: 'is'
פְּרָת; Rashi: from פָּרִין וְרָבִין 'fruitful and many'; the article is lacking

phrases.english: The name of the third river is the Tigris
it is the one that flows east of Assyria

grammar: The third river has the same frame as 2:11 and 2:13; the fourth has no 'name of', only 'the fourth river, it is Perat'.
קִדְמַת is the construct of קִדְמָה, 'east'; Ibn Ezra reads the ת as the sign of a construct standing for the directive ה, 'to the east of Asshur'.
הַהֹלֵךְ is a participle with article: 'the one that goes'.
פְרָת has no 'name of' and no gloss because the river was well known, nearest to the land of Israel (Radak).
Rashi says Cush and Asshur 'did not yet exist': the text writes by the names of the future.
segments.note: 'Tigris' is the familiar English form of חִדֶּקֶל (Hiddekel); 'Euphrates' of פְּרָת (Perat); 'Assyria' of אַשּׁוּר. The meaning of each name goes in the notes, not in the English line (per decisions). The simple clause 'east of Assyria' follows Rashi and Ibn Ezra: toward the east of it, not 'in front of'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: Hiddekel is so named because its waters are sharp (חַדִּין) and swift (קַלִּין); the etymology is kept in the notes.
Rashi: Perat is so named because its waters are fruitful (פָּרִין), multiply (רָבִין) and make people fat; and Cush and Asshur 'did not yet exist': Scripture writes by the future name.
Rashi: קִדְמַת אַשּׁוּר means toward the east of Assyria.
Rashi: the Euphrates is the most important of them all, mentioned by the name of the land of Israel.
Ibn Ezra: the ת of קִדְמַת stands in place of ה, as in וַיֵּרֶד אַבְרָם מִצְרַיְמָה: 'toward the east of Asshur'.
Radak: it goes and extends to the east of the land of Assyria and does not encircle it; it is called Hiddekel from its waters being sharp and swift.
Radak: the Rabbis' two readings of הוּא פְרָת ('it is Perat already' versus 'Perat by itself'); the river is unqualified because it is known on the border of the land of Israel.

segments.english: The LORD God took the human and set him in the garden of Eden to work it and guard it.
segments.literal: and-took the-LORD God ACC the-human and-set-him in-garden-of Eden to-work-it and-to-guard-it

tokens.note: wayyiqtol Qal of לקח; the narrative resumes from 2:8
הָאָדָם with the article: 'the human'
Hiphil wayyiqtol of נוח with a 3rd-person suffix: 'and he made him rest, put him'
construct; גַּן is of either gender, which explains the feminine suffixes after (Ibn Ezra)
infinitive construct with ל and feminine suffix 'it': the garden
infinitive construct with ל and feminine suffix

phrases.literal: 'ACC the-human'; the object marker has no English counterpart

phrases.english: and set him in the garden of Eden
to work it and guard it

grammar: וַיַּנִּחֵהוּ is Hiphil of נוח with a pronominal suffix: 'and he put him to rest, he settled him'; this is a different verb from וַיָּשֶׂם in 2:8.
The feminine suffixes in לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ point to the garden, since גַּן may be feminine (Ibn Ezra); Radak also allows that they point to the ground.
The tevir on וַיִּקַּח and the etnaḥta on הָאָדָם divide the verse into 'took the human' and 'put him in the garden'.
Two infinitives with ל state purpose: 'to work it and to guard it'.
The wayyiqtol chain: took, set. The first repeats the 'put' of 2:8, adding purpose (Radak).
segments.note: The suffix of לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ is feminine; Ibn Ezra takes it to refer to the garden (גַּן being of either gender), against those who refer it to הָאֲדָמָה (the ground), and so the English says 'it'. Ibn Ezra reads 'work' as watering the garden and 'guard' as keeping animals out; the English keeps the wider verbs 'work' and 'guard'. Rashi's 'took him with pleasant words' is a homiletic reading.

commentary.summary: Rashi (Genesis Rabbah): He took him with pleasant words and persuaded him to enter; a homiletic sense of 'took', not adopted in the English.
Ibn Ezra: גַּן is masculine and feminine (plural גַּנִּים and גַּנּוֹת); the suffix in לְעָבְדָהּ is the garden, not the ground: one cannot work a larger place from a smaller one.

Ibn Ezra: לְעָבְדָהּ means to water the garden and לְשָׁמְרָהּ to guard it from the beasts so that they do not enter and defile it; he rejects 'to serve His commandment', since a commandment is not served.
Radak: the feminine suffix can refer to the ground the garden is planted in, or to the garden; the Rabbis read 'work it' as study and 'guard it' as commandments.
Onkelos: וְאַשְׁרֵיהּ בְּגִינְתָא דְעֵדֶן לְמִפְלְחַהּ וּלְמִטְרַהּ: 'and settled him in the garden of Eden to serve it and guard it'.

segments.english: The LORD God commanded the human, saying: "You may eat freely from every tree of the garden."
segments.literal: and-commanded the-LORD God upon the-human to-say from-every-of tree-of the-garden eating you-will-eat

tokens.note: wayyiqtol Piel of צוה; with עַל it introduces a prohibition, as Ibn Ezra notes
עַל after צוה: 'give command upon'
לֵאמֹר, introduces direct speech
partitive מִן: 'from any of'
construct
infinitive absolute: intensifies the finite verb after it
imperfect, 2nd person masculine singular, permissive

phrases.english: "You may eat freely from every tree of the garden."
phrases.literal: 'from-every-of tree-of the-garden eating you-will-eat'; the order is fronted for emphasis

grammar: The infinitive absolute אָכֹל before the finite תֹּאכֵל strengthens it: 'you may eat freely'; Radak compares שָׁמוֹעַ תִּשְׁמְעוּן.
וַיְצַו עַל takes עַל before the person: the idiom opens a command, here a restriction (Ibn Ezra).
The object מִכֹּל עֵץ הַגָּן is fronted, putting the permission first. The imperfect is permissive: 'you may'.
The etnaḥta on לֵאמֹר separates the narrative from the speech.
Because the speech continues in 2:17, the sentence is only the first half of the command.
segments.note: The imperfect with infinitive absolute is rendered as a permission with 'freely'. Ibn Ezra reads the verse as the introduction to the prohibition of 2:17: although fruit of the garden is allowed, the knowledge tree is not. Radak asks whether the command refers to 'you shall not eat' or to both parts. The verse itself carries only the permission. The English line closes the quotation here, as the verse does.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: צִוָּה with עַל means a prohibition, as in עַל הָעָבִים אֲצַוֶּה (Is 5:6); although I have allowed you the fruit of every garden tree, you shall not eat of the fruit of the tree of knowledge.
Radak: the command is either about 'do not eat of it' or both parts, since feeding oneself on what is permitted is itself a command.
Radak: the infinitive absolute with the finite verb strengthens the thing, like שָׁמוֹעַ תִּשְׁמְעוּ.
Sforno: 'from every tree' according to the seasons, as the stars look on, as in לָחֳדָשָׁיו יְבַכֵּר.
